extracted.intended_audience: general public and stakeholders (workers, employers, researchers) seeking an overview of the U.S. Department of Labor
extracted.subtask_description: A concise agency profile describing the Department of Labor's history, mission, subordinate offices, and the types of federal labor protections and programs it administers. Useful for stakeholders preparing comments, research, or seeking contact points within DOL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department mission and core functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Labor (DOL) fosters and promotes the welfare of the job seekers, wage earners, and retirees of the United States by improving their working conditions, advancing their opportunities for profitable employment, protecting their retirement and health care benefits, helping employers find workers, strengthening free collective bargaining, and tracking changes in employment, prices, and other national economic measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement enumerates DOL's central goals and programmatic focus areas — improving working conditions; expanding employment opportunities; protecting retirement and health benefits; assisting employers in hiring; supporting collective bargaining; and collecting/monitoring labor/economic statistics. Use this mission language to understand which issues fall within DOL's purview when preparing comments, requests, or research directed to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal labor laws administered / worker protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department administers a variety of Federal labor laws including those that guarantee workers' rights to safe and healthful working conditions; a minimum hourly wage and overtime pay; freedom from employment discrimination; unemployment insurance; and other income support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This line identifies the substantive statutory areas DOL enforces or oversees: occupational safety and health, wage-and-hour standards (minimum wage/overtime), anti-discrimination in employment, unemployment insurance, and additional income-support programs. When assessing whether an issue or petition should be brought to DOL (or referenced in a comment), align it to one of these statutory domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational components / subordinate offices
rubrics_metrics.description: DOL comprises multiple subordinate agencies and offices (examples listed include: benefits-review-board; disability-employment-policy-office; employee-benefits-security-administration; employees-compensation-appeals-board; employment-and-training-administration; employment-standards-administration; federal-contract-compliance-programs-office; labor-statistics-bureau; labor-management-standards-office; mine-safety-and-health-administration; occupational-safety-and-health-administration; pension-and-welfare-benefits-administration; veterans-employment-and-training-service; wage-and-hour-division; workers-compensation-programs-office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of child offices indicates where specific issues are handled inside DOL (e.g., OSHA for workplace safety, Wage and Hour Division for minimum wage and overtime). Use these component names to target comments or inquiries to the appropriate DOL office rather than the department writ large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and historical establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Labor was created by act of March 4, 1913 (29 U.S.C. 551). A Bureau of Labor was first created by Congress by act of June 24, 1884, in the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank by act of June 13, 1888. It again returned to bureau status in the Department of Commerce and Labor, which was created by act of February 14, 1903 (15 U.S.C. 1501; 29 U.S.C. 1 note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides legal citations and historical context for DOL's establishment and statutory basis. Useful for legal or historical references in regulatory comments or research that require citation to DOL's enabling statutes and historical evolution.
